title: Where Should a Dryer Vent Exit the House?
h1: Where Does a Dryer Vent Go? Where It Should Exit Your House
description: A dryer vent should always end outside, through a wall or roof cap with a working flap. Learn where vents can and cannot go and the signs of a bad setup.
quick_answer: A dryer vent should run from the back of the dryer to the outside of the house and end at a proper vent cap, usually on an exterior wall or the roof. It should never end in the attic, garage, crawl space or inside a wall. Shorter, straighter runs with smooth metal duct work best.
body:
A dryer pushes out hot, damp, lint-filled air every time it runs. That air has to leave the house completely. If it ends up in an attic, garage or wall cavity, the moisture and lint stay behind, and both cause problems: mold, rot, dust and a real fire risk.

In most San Diego and Orange County homes the vent goes one of three ways: straight out a nearby exterior wall, up through the attic and out the roof, or under the floor and out the side of the house. Which one you have usually depends on where the laundry sits.

Where is the best place for a dryer vent to exit?

The best exit is the one that gives the shortest, straightest path outdoors. For a laundry room on an outside wall, that's usually a wall cap a few feet from the dryer. For a laundry closet in the middle of the house or on a second floor, the vent often has to go up through the attic and out the roof.

A good termination has a few things in common:

  • It's fully outdoors. The cap is on the exterior of the house, not inside a soffit, eave or attic space.
  • It has a flap or damper. The flap opens when the dryer runs and closes to keep out wind, rain, birds and rodents.
  • It has no screen. Screens catch lint and clog quickly. A bird guard designed for dryer vents is different, but a plain mesh screen is a problem.
  • It's away from openings. The cap should sit a few feet away from windows, doors and air intakes so the damp exhaust doesn't drift back inside.
  • It's easy to reach. You'll want to check and clean it, so a cap you can see and get to is a plus.

Where should a dryer vent never go?

We still find vents ending in spots that look convenient but cause trouble. A dryer vent should never:

  • End in the attic, even if it's pointed at a roof vent or soffit. Lint piles up on insulation and the moisture soaks the roof deck.
  • Exhaust into the garage, a crawl space or under the house.
  • Blow into a wall or ceiling cavity.
  • Connect to a chimney, plumbing vent or another exhaust duct.
  • Use an indoor lint box or "vent diverter" for a gas dryer. Gas dryers produce combustion gases that must go outside.

If you've found a vent that just stops in the attic, that's worth fixing right away, along with cleaning up any lint that has settled on the insulation.

Wall vent or roof vent: which is better?

A sidewall vent is usually better when the laundry is near an outside wall. The run is shorter, the cap is easy to inspect, and lint doesn't have to be pushed straight up against gravity.

Roof vents are common in condos, townhomes and two-story houses where the dryer is upstairs or in an interior closet. They work fine when they're installed with the right roof cap and kept clean, but they clog faster. Lint tends to collect at the bottom of the vertical run and at the cap, and roof caps are harder to check. Many have small louvers or screens that trap lint, so if you have a roof vent, plan on more frequent cleaning.

What kind of duct should the vent use?

The duct itself matters as much as the exit point. Inside the walls, attic or floor, the vent should be smooth-wall rigid metal duct, typically 4 inches in diameter. Joints should be taped with foil tape, not held together with screws that poke into the duct and snag lint.

The short connector behind the dryer can be a flexible metal transition hose, but it should be as short as possible and not crushed when the dryer is pushed back. White vinyl or thin foil accordion hose should be replaced. It sags, traps lint and can tear.

Code and the dryer manufacturer both limit how long the vent can be and how many elbows it can have, because every bend slows the airflow. If your run is long or has several turns, a booster fan or a reroute may be needed. Your dryer's installation manual lists its limits.

How can I tell if my dryer vent is set up wrong?

A few signs point to a vent that's in the wrong place, too long or blocked:

  1. Clothes take more than one cycle to dry.
  2. The laundry room feels hot or humid when the dryer runs.
  3. You smell a burning or musty odor during drying.
  4. Lint collects around the dryer or at the outside cap.
  5. You can't find where the vent comes out of the house.
  6. The outside flap barely moves while the dryer is running.

That last check is easy. Start the dryer, go outside and hold your hand near the cap. You should feel strong, warm airflow. Weak airflow means a clog, a crushed section or a disconnected joint somewhere along the way.

Can a dryer vent be moved?

Yes. Rerouting a vent is common when a home has a long, twisting run, a vent that ends in the attic, or a laundry that was moved during a remodel. The goal is to cut the length and the number of turns, or to switch from a hard-to-reach roof exit to a sidewall exit when the layout allows it.

faqs: Can a dryer vent go into the attic?

No. The vent has to pass through the attic and end outside at a roof or wall cap. A vent that stops in the attic leaves lint on the insulation and soaks the roof deck with moisture, which leads to mold and a fire risk.
Can I vent my dryer into the garage?
No. A garage counts as part of the house for venting. The moist air and lint will build up there, and a gas dryer also releases combustion gases that need to go fully outdoors.
Should a dryer vent cap have a screen?
No. A plain screen catches lint and clogs quickly, which slows the dryer and raises the fire risk. Use a cap with a flap or damper that opens when the dryer runs and closes when it stops.
How often should I clean a dryer vent?

Most homes do well with a cleaning about once a year. Long runs, roof vents, big families and homes with pets usually need it more often. If drying times start creeping up, don't wait for the calendar.
